This paper tackles an important and underexplored problem: moving spoken dialogue agents beyond turn-based, half-duplex interaction toward genuinely synchronous, full-duplex behavior with overlaps, backchannels, and latency-aware turn-taking. The central idea is to adapt a pretrained autoregressive LLM so that it operates against a real-world clock by interleaving two speakers’ speech-unit streams in fixed-duration chunks, marked by periodic synchronization tokens. The paper further proposes a three-stage training recipe that relies heavily on synthetic spoken dialogue derived from text corpora, followed by relatively modest fine-tuning on real dual-channel conversational speech. Empirically, the paper reports substantial gains over dGSLM in semantic meaningfulness while maintaining comparable or slightly better turn-taking naturalness, and also presents simulated interaction experiments under one-chunk latency.

Overall, I find the paper ambitious, timely, and conceptually interesting. The problem formulation is compelling, and the proposed framing of synchrony as chunked autoregressive generation with explicit periodic timing markers is elegant. The work also has practical significance: many current “voice assistants” are indeed still turn-based systems with endpointing heuristics, and a method that can support continuous listening and speaking would be a meaningful step forward. The empirical results, especially the large gap in human-rated meaningfulness relative to dGSLM, suggest that leveraging text-pretrained LLMs is a promising direction for spoken dialogue modeling.

The strongest aspect of the paper is the combination of a simple architectural adaptation with a pragmatic training pipeline. Rather than designing a bespoke speech-only architecture, the authors preserve the standard decoder-only LLM setup and encode synchrony through sequence formatting. This is appealing because it inherits the semantic strengths of large text-pretrained models. The use of periodic speaker tags as coarse timing anchors is also a neat idea: it gives the model a notion of elapsed time without requiring continuous-time modeling or specialized recurrent machinery. The latency-tolerant interaction mechanism, where the model predicts an estimated user chunk before generating its own next chunk, is also intuitively well motivated by human anticipatory turn-taking.

A second major strength is the paper’s emphasis on full-duplex interaction as distinct from merely streaming or low-latency turn-taking. Many prior systems claim conversationality while still relying on explicit turn boundaries. This paper clearly articulates why full-duplex dialogue is qualitatively different and why overlap, backchanneling, and interruption matter. The framing is persuasive and grounded in conversation analysis literature.

The empirical story is also reasonably strong at a high level. The human evaluation indicates a very large improvement in meaningfulness over dGSLM, while naturalness remains roughly comparable. The out-of-distribution evaluation on CANDOR is a useful addition and supports the claim that text-pretrained semantics plus synthetic dialogue pretraining improve generalization. The interaction-mode experiments are also valuable because they move beyond offline continuation and attempt to validate the latency-aware mechanism.

That said, I have several substantive concerns about the methodology and evaluation that limit how strongly I can trust the conclusions in their current form.

My main concern is that the comparison to dGSLM may not be fully controlled, and the paper sometimes attributes gains to the synchrony mechanism when they may primarily come from text-pretrained semantics and large-scale synthetic data. In fact, the paper’s own narrative suggests that the biggest advantage over dGSLM is semantic coherence inherited from Llama3 plus 212k hours of synthetic speech generated from text dialogue. This is a meaningful contribution, but it is somewhat orthogonal to the core technical claim about synchronous full-duplex modeling. As written, it is difficult to disentangle how much of the improvement comes from: the chunked synchronous representation, the deduplication scheme, the three-stage curriculum, the use of Llama3 initialization, or simply much larger and richer supervision than the baseline effectively receives. A stronger paper would include ablations isolating these factors, especially comparisons against turn-based or non-synchronous LLM-based spoken dialogue baselines trained with the same synthetic data pipeline.

Relatedly, the paper would benefit from a more direct baseline against a strong cascaded or speech-text LLM system adapted for streaming interaction. dGSLM is a reasonable historical baseline for full-duplex spoken dialogue, but it is also a speech-only model from an earlier generation. Since the paper’s main empirical advantage appears to be semantic quality, a more contemporary baseline would be important. For example, one would like to know how much is gained over a strong turn-based spoken LLM with incremental ASR/TTS and a learned turn-taking policy, or over a decoder-only speech-text model without the proposed synchronization-token scheme. Without such baselines, the paper convincingly shows superiority to dGSLM, but not necessarily to the broader state of the art in practical spoken dialogue systems.

A second major concern is the evaluation protocol for semantics. The paper transcribes generated spoken dialogues with ASR, discards overlapping speech, converts them into turn-based text dialogues, and then computes perplexity under a text dialogue model. This is at best an indirect proxy for semantic quality. It may systematically favor outputs that are easy to transcribe and structurally similar to text dialogue, while underrepresenting the very phenomena the paper claims to model, such as overlap and backchanneling. Discarding overlap is especially problematic in a paper about full-duplex dialogue, because overlap may carry meaningful pragmatic content. Moreover, perplexity under a text dialogue model is not a standard or obviously calibrated measure of dialogue quality. It would help to know which text model is used, how sensitive results are to that choice, and whether ASR errors differ across systems. Human meaningfulness ratings partly address this issue, but the automatic semantic metric remains somewhat hard to interpret.

My third concern is about the naturalness evaluation. The paper follows dGSLM in correlating average durations of IPUs, pauses, and FTOs between generated continuations and ground-truth continuations conditioned on the same prompt. This is a useful diagnostic, but it is not a direct measure of conversational naturalness. Correlation of aggregate durations can be gamed by matching marginal statistics without producing locally appropriate turn-taking behavior. Also, the reported correlations are still fairly low in absolute terms, especially for FTO, which is arguably the most central measure for overlap/gap timing. The human naturalness MOS is therefore important, but the reported differences are small and in some cases slightly favor dGSLM or re-synthesized references. The paper’s claim that SyncLLM “maintains naturalness” is fair; stronger claims of improved naturalness would not be justified.

A fourth concern is that the interaction experiments are still simulations between two models rather than real human-agent interaction. This is understandable for a first paper, but it weakens the practical claim of full-duplex usability under internet-scale latency. In particular, the user-side speech in the interaction setting is generated by another SyncLLM instance, which likely shares the same tokenization assumptions, timing regularities, and conversational priors. This may make the interaction problem easier than real deployment with human users, disfluencies, ASR noise, microphone artifacts, and unpredictable interruptions. The paper should be more explicit that this is a proof-of-concept simulation rather than a demonstration of robust real-world full-duplex interaction.

There are also several technical details that need clarification.

First, the interpolation heuristic from deduplicated tokens back to fixed-rate HuBERT sequences seems potentially lossy in a way that could affect prosody and timing. The paper states that errors are imperceptible even at 240 ms chunk size, but this claim is not rigorously evaluated. Since the method’s timing fidelity is central, I would like to see either objective reconstruction metrics or a targeted perceptual study comparing interpolation strategies and chunk sizes.

Second, the choice to always include one speaker tag per chunk but omit the other when there are no novel tokens is clever, but it introduces asymmetry into the representation. It is not obvious whether this biases the model toward one speaker role or affects generation stability. Some discussion or ablation on symmetric alternatives would be useful.

Third, the latency model assumes one-chunk delayed access and uses predicted user chunks to bridge the gap. But actual cloud deployment latency is variable and includes ASR/tokenization delay, network jitter, and synthesis delay. The paper maps chunk size to “resiliency” up to 240 ms, but this seems simplified. It would help to specify the full latency budget and whether generation plus vocoding can actually complete within the chunk duration on realistic hardware.

Fourth, the training data description is somewhat confusing. The abstract mentions 212k hours of synthetic spoken dialogue and 2k hours of real-world spoken dialogue, while Table 1 lists 193k + 20k synthetic hours and 1927 real hours. This is close, but the exact accounting should be made consistent. More importantly, the text datasets used in stages 1 and 2 are only loosely described. Since synthetic data is central to the contribution, the paper should provide clearer provenance, filtering criteria, dialogue length statistics, and perhaps examples of the generated speech/dialogue formatting.

Fifth, the human evaluation setup is useful but somewhat limited. Each item is rated by only three annotators, and the paper reports means of item-level medians. That is acceptable, but more detail on inter-rater agreement, prompt selection, and whether raters heard stereo/separate channels would help. Since naturalness in duplex dialogue depends on overlap perception, the presentation format matters a lot. It would also be useful to know whether raters were instructed to judge speech quality separately from dialogue timing, since vocoder quality may confound naturalness judgments.

I also think the paper somewhat overstates novelty in places. The core mechanism is not a new architecture so much as a new sequence representation and training/inference procedure for standard autoregressive LLMs. That is still valuable, but the contribution should be framed precisely. Similarly, “LLMs do not have a sense of time” is a reasonable intuition, but the proposed solution gives only coarse discretized timing tied to chunk boundaries, not a general temporal grounding mechanism.

Despite these concerns, I think the paper has real merit. The idea is simple, plausible, and potentially impactful. The results strongly suggest that bringing text-pretrained LLMs into spoken full-duplex dialogue is worthwhile, and the synchronization-token formulation is a promising way to do so. The paper is also refreshingly focused on an interaction property that matters in practice and is often ignored in benchmark-driven work.

To strengthen the paper, I would most strongly recommend the following additions or revisions. First, include ablations that isolate the contribution of synchrony modeling from the contribution of text-pretrained semantics and synthetic data. For example: a turn-based spoken LLM baseline with the same stage-1 training; a model trained without periodic synchronization tokens; a model trained without deduplication; and a comparison between continuation-only and latency-aware interaction training/inference. Second, compare against at least one stronger contemporary baseline, ideally a cascaded streaming system or a speech-text LLM adapted for incremental dialogue. Third, provide more direct evaluation of overlap/backchannel behavior, such as precision/recall or distributional matching for backchannels, interruption timing, overlap ratio, and response latency conditioned on conversational cues. Fourth, clarify the deployment latency assumptions and report actual runtime measurements. Fifth, expand the discussion of limitations around simulated interaction and the absence of real human-agent studies.

In summary, this is a strong and interesting paper with a compelling problem statement and a clever, practical approach. Its main empirical message—that LLM-based synchronous spoken dialogue can substantially improve semantic meaningfulness while preserving turn-taking naturalness—is promising and likely true. However, the current evaluation does not fully disentangle the source of gains, and the baseline set is not strong enough to conclusively establish superiority of the proposed synchrony mechanism itself. I view this as a valuable contribution that is close to the bar for a top-tier venue, but it would benefit significantly from stronger controlled comparisons and more targeted evaluation of full-duplex behavior.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper proposes SyncLLM, a decoder-only LLM-based framework for full-duplex spoken dialogue that explicitly incorporates wall-clock synchrony via periodic speaker/synchronization tokens and chunked interleaving of both speakers’ speech-unit streams. The method uses deduplicated HuBERT tokens to improve semantic efficiency, predicts future user chunks to tolerate one-chunk latency, and is trained with a three-stage recipe combining large-scale synthetic spoken dialogue from text data with about 2k hours of real dual-channel dialogue. Experiments compare against dGSLM on semantic proxies, turn-taking statistics, and human MOS, showing substantially improved perceived meaningfulness while roughly matching naturalness, plus simulated interaction under 160–240ms latency.
strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: moving from turn-based/half-duplex spoken agents to genuinely synchronous full-duplex dialogue.
Conceptually novel formulation of synchrony for autoregressive LLMs using periodic synchronization/speaker tokens and chunked interleaving tied to wall-clock time.
Practical latency-aware design: predicting the user’s current chunk to generate the agent’s next chunk is a reasonable mechanism for coping with network delay.
Strong engineering contribution in adapting a pretrained text LLM (Llama3-8B) to spoken full-duplex dialogue while leveraging text pretraining.
Three-stage training recipe is sensible and data-efficient, using large synthetic speech corpora to compensate for scarce real duplex dialogue data.
Empirical results are promising: large gains over dGSLM in meaningfulness MOS and better semantic proxy scores, while maintaining similar naturalness.
Includes both in-distribution and OOD evaluation (Fisher/CANDOR) and a simulated interaction setting rather than only offline continuation.
Paper clearly motivates why half-duplex assumptions are limiting for spoken interaction and why timing/synchrony matter.
weaknesses: The central empirical comparisons are mostly against a single prior baseline (dGSLM); comparisons to stronger modern speech-text or spoken dialogue systems are limited or absent.

Several evaluation choices are indirect or potentially weak proxies: semantic quality is measured via ASR transcription followed by perplexity under a text dialogue model, which may conflate ASR errors, overlap removal, and language-model bias.
The naturalness metric based on Pearson correlation of average event durations with ground-truth continuations is unusual and may not strongly validate conversational realism or appropriateness.

The interaction setting is only simulated via LLM-LLM interaction with one-chunk latency; there is no real-time human-agent deployment study demonstrating actual end-to-end latency, robustness, or user experience.
The interpolation heuristic from deduplicated tokens back to fixed-rate HuBERT sequences is ad hoc, and the claim that resulting errors are imperceptible is not rigorously validated.

The paper lacks detailed ablations isolating the contributions of key components: synchronization tokens, deduplication, future-user prediction, synthetic-data stages, chunk size, and real-data fine-tuning.
Human evaluation uses only 3 raters per item and relatively small scale; significance testing between close naturalness scores is not clearly established.
Speech quality is acknowledged as limited, which may affect perceived naturalness and practical usability.
methodological_flaws: The semantic evaluation pipeline is scientifically weak as a direct measure of dialogue quality: generated speech is ASR-transcribed, overlaps are ignored, and perplexity is computed under a text-only dialogue model. This may systematically favor models whose outputs are easier for ASR/text LM pipelines rather than genuinely better full-duplex spoken dialogue.

The turn-taking evaluation computes Pearson correlation between average event durations in generations and ground-truth continuations for the same prompts. Correlation of aggregated durations does not establish that generated turn-taking is contextually appropriate, human-like, or causally aligned with prompt content; it is a limited proxy and may be insensitive to important failure modes.

The interpolation procedure equally repeats deduplicated tokens within a chunk to reconstruct timing, despite acknowledging mismatch with original durations. Since timing is central to the paper’s claim, this heuristic introduces an unquantified source of temporal distortion without objective reconstruction-error analysis or perceptual validation beyond anecdotal observation.

The latency-tolerance claim is only validated in simulation with one-chunk delayed model-model interaction, not with real networked streaming infrastructure. Thus the conclusion about robustness to Internet-scale latencies is only partially supported empirically.

The paper does not provide enough controlled ablations to justify causal attribution of gains to the proposed synchrony mechanism versus simpler explanations such as stronger pretrained backbone, much larger synthetic training data, or different tokenization/training recipes.

Comparison fairness is somewhat unclear: dGSLM is an older speech-only architecture, while SyncLLM benefits from a large pretrained text LLM and extensive synthetic data. Without stronger matched baselines or ablations, the scientific claim that synchrony modeling itself drives the gains is not fully established.
